Whole-lesson orientation

Skeletal Muscle Relaxants

p. 1

The lecture divides skeletal muscle relaxants into two broad groups. Neuromuscular blockers produce skeletal muscle paralysis for intubation, surgery, and ICU use. Spasmolytics and antispasmodics reduce spasticity or painful muscle spasm in different clinical settings.

Lesson begins here

Cholinergic Transmission and Normal Neuromuscular Function

p. 1

Where the lecture places cholinergic transmission

  • All preganglionic efferent autonomic fibers use nicotinic transmission. The lecture labels the neuronal receptor as NN.
  • The neuronal nicotinic receptor is a pentameric receptor and the lecture notes α- and β-type subunits in the ANS.
  • The lecture also notes that postganglionic sympathetic fibers to sweat glands use muscarinic receptors.
  • Somatic motor fibers to skeletal muscle use the muscle-type nicotinic receptor, labeled NM. It is a ligand-gated ion channel.

Normal neuromuscular sequence

p. 1
1
Nerve action potential arrives at the motor nerve terminal.
2
Calcium enters the nerve terminal and promotes fusion of ACh-containing vesicles with the surface membrane.
3
Acetylcholine is released into the synaptic cleft.
4
ACh binds nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate and produces a conformational change that permits sodium entry.
5
The channel opens and Na and K move across the channel.
6
Depolarization creates the motor action potential.
7
Muscle contraction follows the sodium-associated depolarizing event described in the lecture.
8
Acetylcholinesterase removes ACh by degrading it into choline and acetate.

Muscle-type nicotinic receptor

p. 2
  • The adult muscle end-plate nicotinic receptor has 5 subunits: 2α, β, γ, and δ.
  • There are 2 ACh binding sites at the α-β and δ-α interfaces.
  • Binding at one site increases receptor affinity for a second ACh molecule. With both sites occupied, the channel opens and sodium enters.
  • Presynaptic motor axon terminal receptors promote additional ACh transmitter release.
  • Extrajunctional receptors are not usually involved in normal neuromuscular transmission. They proliferate during prolonged immobilization, paralysis due to stroke, bedridden states, and thermal burns.
Study aid
Two ACh molecules are needed to open the normal muscle nicotinic receptor.
That same two-site architecture explains why occupancy of even one site by a nondepolarizing blocker can prevent channel opening later in the lecture.
Basic pharmacology

General Features of Neuromuscular Blockers

p. 2

Chemical structure and distribution

  • Neuromuscular blockers show a resemblance to acetylcholine.
  • Succinylcholine is described as two acetylcholine-like molecules joined together.
  • Pancuronium has a steroidal framework plus two acetylcholine-like portions in its structure.
  • These drugs have 1 or 2 quaternary nitrogens, which makes them polar and poorly lipid soluble.
  • Poor lipid solubility means poor gastrointestinal absorption. The lecture therefore emphasizes parenteral preparations.
  • Polarity limits entry into the CNS and contributes to a limited volume of distribution of 80–140 mL/kg.

Depolarizing NMB

Succinylcholine or suxamethonium is the lecture's clinically available depolarizing blocker.

Nondepolarizing NMB

Agents such as rocuronium, vecuronium, pancuronium, atracurium, cisatracurium, tubocurarine, and mivacurium are organized by structure and duration.

Clinical relevance
Neuromuscular blockers produce paralysis, not central anesthesia.
The lecture repeatedly notes their poor CNS access because of high polarity and quaternary nitrogens.
Clinical uses are intubation, intraoperative skeletal muscle relaxation, and ICU control of mechanical ventilation.
Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker

Succinylcholine: Pharmacokinetics and Prolonged Block

p. 3
Must Know
Succinylcholine is the only clinically available depolarizing neuromuscular blocker in the lecture.
Route: IV or IM.
IV administration gives 100% bioavailability in plasma.

Metabolism

Succinylcholine
→
PseudocholinesteraseRapid plasma hydrolysis
→
SuccinylmonocholineActive metabolite
→
Succinic acid + choline
  • Rapid hydrolysis occurs in the plasma before much drug reaches the NMJ.
  • Butyrylcholinesterase, found in the liver, is also described as participating in metabolism.
  • Drug that reaches the NMJ eventually diffuses away from the motor end plate, where degradation contributes to termination of action.
  • Metabolites are excreted in urine.
Onset60–90 sec
Duration5–10 min
Lecture emphasisShortest duration among the NMBs discussed

Factors that decrease pseudocholinesterase activity or level

  • Conditions: pregnancy, burns, oral contraceptives, MAOI use.
  • Diseases: liver disease and neoplastic diseases.
  • Medications: anticholinesterases, echothiopate, cytotoxic drugs, tetrahydroaminacrine, and hexafluorenium.
  • Neostigmine inhibits pseudocholinesterase and can prolong succinylcholine block.
Atypical pseudocholinesterase and the dibucaine number
FormIncidence in lectureDibucaine numberExpected succinylcholine block
Homozygous typicalNormal70–80Normal duration
Heterozygous atypical1/48050–60Increased by about 50–100%
Homozygous atypical1/3,20020–30May last 4–8 hours
Clinical cue
Dibucaine inhibits the normal enzyme much more than the abnormal enzyme.
A higher dibucaine number corresponds to typical enzyme activity in the lecture.
With prolonged paralysis from atypical pseudocholinesterase, mechanical ventilation may be required.
Mechanism and pharmacodynamics

Succinylcholine: Phase I, Phase II, Effects, and Interactions

p. 3

Phase I block: depolarizing block

1
Succinylcholine binds nAChRs at the motor end plate.
2
Depolarization occurs, followed by fasciculations.
3
Because succinylcholine is hydrolyzed more slowly than ACh, it remains associated with the receptor longer.
4
The membrane remains depolarized and becomes unresponsive to incoming impulses.
5
No repolarization and no effective excitation-contraction coupling occur, producing flaccid paralysis.

Phase II block: desensitizing block

  • Not usually seen.
  • Occurs with continuous exposure, high doses, or prolonged infusion of succinylcholine.
  • The muscle membrane becomes repolarized but desensitized to incoming impulses.
  • The muscle remains paralyzed and the block behaves later like a nondepolarizing block.

Cardiovascular and other effects

p. 4
  • Cardiac arrhythmias, especially when administered with halothane. The lecture lists sinus bradycardia, nodal rhythm, and ventricular arrhythmias.
  • Hyperkalemia. A transient potassium increase can become dangerous in patients with burns, trauma, nerve damage, neuromuscular disease, renal failure, or metabolic acidosis.
  • Increased intraocular pressure. Onset is under 60 seconds, lasts about 2–4 minutes, declines by 5 minutes, and returns to normal. The lecture advises against succinylcholine in open eye injury and increased intraocular pressure such as glaucoma.
  • Increased intragastric pressure due to abdominal fasciculations. This can promote regurgitation, vomiting, aspiration, and anesthetic complications in a patient with a full stomach.
  • Postoperative muscle pain may follow fasciculations.
  • Malignant hyperthermia can occur in susceptible patients.

Drug interactions and defasciculation

  • Succinylcholine + neostigmine can prolong the succinylcholine block because neostigmine also inhibits pseudocholinesterase.
  • A small dose of a nondepolarizing NMB before succinylcholine can prevent fasciculations.
  • This defasciculating strategy is emphasized when fasciculations and increased intragastric pressure are undesirable, such as in a patient with a full stomach.
Lecture-specific note
The page 4 bullet states that combining a nondepolarizing blocker with succinylcholine increases the succinylcholine dose requirement by about 5%.
A lecturer note on the same page states that the depolarizing NMB dose must be increased by about 50%.
This reviewer preserves both lecture statements without reconciling them.

Absorption and distribution

  • These drugs are highly polar because of one or two quaternary nitrogens.
  • They are inactive orally and therefore use parenteral preparations.
  • They do not readily cross membranes and have poor CNS access.
  • They have a limited volume of distribution.
  • They undergo a rapid initial distribution phase followed by a slower elimination phase.

Metabolism

  • Steroidal derivatives such as rocuronium, vecuronium, and pancuronium undergo hepatic metabolism. Their duration can be prolonged with liver pathology.
  • The lecture describes a 3-hydroxymetabolite with about 40–80% of the potency of the parent drug. At high concentrations it can contribute to prolonged paralysis.
  • Isoquinoline derivatives atracurium and cisatracurium undergo hepatic metabolism and spontaneous plasma degradation called Hofmann elimination.
  • 📌 Hofmann elimination Spontaneous plasma degradation is useful in patients with hepatic or kidney pathology because elimination can still occur in plasma.
  • Cisatracurium is described as less dependent on hepatic metabolism and as producing less laudanosine with less histamine release than atracurium.
  • Laudanosine has a half-life of about 150 minutes, can cross the BBB, and can accumulate during prolonged atracurium infusion in the ICU. The lecture associates high concentrations with CNS excitatory effects, seizures, and increased anesthetic requirements.
  • Gantacurium is presented as experimental and not clinically available. Its metabolism is non-enzymatic and histamine release may cause hypotension at ED95.
Study aid
Structure grouping from the lecture:
Rocuronium, Vecuronium, Pancuronium = steroidal derivatives.
Tubocurarine, Atracurium, Cisatracurium = isoquinoline derivatives.
Mechanism, adverse effects, interactions, special populations

Nondepolarizing Neuromuscular Blockers

p. 5

Main mechanism: competitive antagonism

  • Nondepolarizing NMBs compete with acetylcholine at the nicotinic receptor.
  • Occupancy of even one binding site by a nondepolarizing blocker is enough to prevent opening of the receptor-ion channel.
  • Acetylcholinesterase rapidly degrades ACh in the synaptic cleft.
  • At large doses, nondepolarizing blockers can also block ion-channel pores and interfere with prejunctional Na+ channels, reducing ACh release.
  • The lecture explicitly states that the main mechanism remains competitive antagonism at the nicotinic receptor.

Rocuronium
Vecuronium		Presented as preferred choices when minimal cardiovascular disturbance is desired.

Tubocurarine		Histamine release causes vasodilation and tachycardia. Antihistamines can attenuate the effect.
Ganglionic blockadeTubocurarine
Metocurine		Especially described with larger doses.

Must Know
📌 Lecture high-yield Steroidal-type NMBs are stated not to cause histamine release.
Histamine release ranking in the lecture: D-tubocurarine > metocurine > atracurium/mivacurium > cisatracurium.
Histamine release may cause flushing, hypotension, bronchospasm, and tachycardia.

Drug interactions that enhance nondepolarizing blockade

  • Inhaled anesthetics: Isoflurane > Sevoflurane > Desflurane > Halothane > N2O.
  • Aminoglycosides: streptomycin, gentamicin, amikacin.
  • Macrolide: erythromycin.
  • Local anesthetics: at high doses, they can block sodium channels and neuromuscular transmission.

Effects of disease and age

📌 Myasthenia gravis Myasthenia gravis

Antibodies reduce functional nicotinic ACh receptors. The lecture states that patients are less susceptible to depolarizing NMBs because fewer receptors are available for fasciculation and paralysis, and more susceptible to nondepolarizing NMBs because fewer remaining receptors need to be blocked.

📌 Severe burns and UMN disease Severe burns or upper motor neuron disease

The lecture advises that these patients should not receive depolarizing NMBs. They appear resistant to nondepolarizing blockers because extrajunctional receptors proliferate, increasing the number of nicotinic receptors that must be occupied.

📌 Elderly >70 years Elderly patients

Decreased liver and kidney clearance can prolong duration of nondepolarizing blockade. The lecture therefore states that these patients need lower doses.

Clinical pharmacology

Intubation, Intraoperative Use, ICU Use, and Neuromuscular Monitoring

p. 6

Clinical uses of neuromuscular blockers

  • Intubation of the trachea through production of muscle paralysis and relaxation.
  • Intraoperative skeletal muscle relaxation to improve exposure of the operative field, including relaxation of abdominal muscles.
  • ICU control of mechanical ventilation.
  • NMBs do not have central activity because their polarity and quaternary nitrogens limit CNS access.

COVID-19 intubation considerations in the lecture

  • Main goal: prevent aerosolization.
  • Patient should be in deep sleep.
  • Use deep and rapid neuromuscular blockade. The lecture states that a full dose of either a depolarizing or nondepolarizing NMB may be used.
  • The most experienced intubator, usually the anesthesiologist, should perform the procedure to maximize first-attempt success.
  • Use specialized equipment such as video laryngoscopy.
  • Avoid high O2 flow, excess non-essential personnel, and a patient who is inadequately asleep or paralyzed.
Clinical pearl: exploratory laparotomy
Intubation: Either depolarizing or nondepolarizing NMB can be used when rapid intubation is the goal.
Intraoperative abdominal relaxation: Nondepolarizing blockers are ideal because of longer duration. The lecture commonly uses the intermediate group with a 20–35 minute duration.
Postoperative mechanical ventilation: The lecture states that NMB use may continue when needed.
If ventilation is not needed: A reversal agent is given at the end of surgery. Cholinesterase inhibitors are paired with an antimuscarinic to counter muscarinic adverse effects. Sugammadex is used when the NMB is steroidal.

Nerve stimulation

  • A nerve stimulator delivers transdermal electrical stimulation to a superficial nerve supplying a muscle.
  • The lecture calls ulnar nerve–adductor pollicis stimulation the gold standard for assessing neuromuscular function in anesthesia.
  • Stimulation produces contraction or adduction of the thumb and allows assessment of the degree of paralysis.
  • Other nerves mentioned are the posterior tibial nerve and facial nerve.

Train-of-four pattern

  • Four maximal electrical stimulations are given to the ulnar nerve and the adductor pollicis contractions are observed.
  • No blocker: four equal-amplitude contractions.
  • After rocuronium: the contractions show fade, with the fourth twitch smaller than the first.
  • The lecture states that only nondepolarizing blockers produce fade. Depolarizing blockers produce equal diminution of amplitudes.
  • As blockade deepens, TOF count falls from 4 to 3 to 1 to 0.
  • 📌 Complete block TOFR 0 is presented as the point of complete paralysis and the best time for intubation.
  • 📌 Recovery threshold TOFR >90% is required for recovery from neuromuscular blockade.
Reversal of nondepolarizing blockade

Cholinesterase Inhibitors and Sugammadex

p. 7

Cholinesterase inhibitors

  • Decrease degradation of ACh.
  • More ACh competes with the nondepolarizing blocker and reverses the block.
  • Neostigmine is the IV preparation listed.
  • Pyridostigmine is also used.
  • Both are stated to increase ACh release from the presynaptic motor nerve ending.

Edrophonium

  • Short-acting.
  • Not used for reversal of NMB blockade in the lecture.
  • Usually used for the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.
Why an antimuscarinic is paired with a cholinesterase inhibitor
Increasing ACh also increases muscarinic effects.
The lecture highlights bradycardia and increased gastrointestinal secretions as reasons to give an antimuscarinic agent with a cholinesterase inhibitor.

Sugammadex

  • Rapidly reverses blockade from steroidal-type nondepolarizing NMBs, including rocuronium, vecuronium, and pancuronium in the lecture.
  • Forms a 1:1 tight-binding complex with rocuronium in plasma.
  • The lecture describes sugammadex as 18× faster in onset than neostigmine.
  • Returns TOF ratio to >0.90.
  • Described as a sugar compound, gamma dextran.
Sugammadex binds plasma rocuronium
→
Plasma rocuronium falls
→
Concentration gradient increases
→
Rocuronium leaves the NMJ for plasma
→
More rocuronium is bound

Elimination and cautions

  • The sugammadex–rocuronium complex is excreted in urine within 24 hours under normal renal function in the lecture.
  • 📌 Severe renal impairment Excretion is impaired in severe renal impairment, so the complex stays longer in plasma.
  • The lecture notes approval in Europe in 2008 and US FDA approval in 2016. It also states that sugammadex is FDA-approved in the Philippines.

📌 Adverse effects Adverse effects and interactions

  • Hypersensitivity with nausea, pruritus, and urticaria.
  • Anaphylaxis.
  • Rare bradycardia leading to cardiac arrest.
  • Coagulopathy has also been reported in the lecture.
  • Sugammadex may bind progesterone-based contraceptives, producing an effect similar to missing 1–2 doses. The lecture advises alternative non-progesterone contraception for 7 days.
  • Toremifene can displace rocuronium from the sugammadex complex. The lecture links this to prolonged neuromuscular block and decreased toremifene efficacy.
Spasticity treatment

Spasmolytics

p. 8

📌 Spasmolytics Spasmolytics

Used for spasticity from UMN lesions, involuntary skeletal muscle contractions, and hyperactivity of α-motor neurons. Some have central adverse effects such as sedation and dizziness.

📌 Antispasmodics Antispasmodics

Used for spasms from peripheral musculoskeletal conditions, such as whiplash injury. Some also cause sedation and dizziness.

General spasmolytic features

  • Provide relief from painful muscle spasms.
  • The lecture states that they do not provide much improvement in function such as moving about or working.
  • Central adverse effects such as sedation and dizziness may limit functional status.
  • 📌 Centrally acting Diazepam, baclofen, tizanidine.
  • 📌 Peripherally acting Dantrolene sodium, eperisone HCl, pherinamidol.

Available oral and IV/IM.

Dantrolene and ryanodine receptors

  • Dantrolene blocks skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling by reducing calcium release from the SR.
  • The lecture associates skeletal muscle action with RYR1.
  • Cardiac smooth muscle is described as containing the RYR2 isoform and being slightly depressed.

📌 Other centrally acting spasmolytic drugs Other centrally acting drugs in the lecture

  • Gabapentin: antiseizure drug with voltage-gated Ca++ channel antagonism. The lecture notes a spasmolytic effect, especially in multiple sclerosis.
  • Pregabalin: antiseizure drug and voltage-gated Ca++ channel antagonist. Analog of gabapentin.
  • Progabide: GABAA and GABAB agonist.
  • Glycine: inhibitory amino acid neurotransmitter with more action at the spinal cord. The lecture states that progabide and glycine readily cross the BBB and are not available in the Philippines.
  • Idrocilamide and riluzole: newer drugs for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in the lecture. They inhibit glutamatergic transmission and are described as not commercially available in the Philippines.
High-yield complications and local chemodenervation

Malignant Hyperthermia and Botulinum Toxin

p. 9

Malignant hyperthermia

Susceptible patientRare familial or genetic condition
↓
Trigger exposureSuccinylcholine or inhalational anesthetics
↓
Uncontrolled Ca++ release from SR
↓
Continuous excitation-contraction couplingHypermetabolic state
↓
↑ CO2 and pCO2, acidosis, arrhythmiasHyperthermia is a late sign
  • The defect is located at chromosome 19q13.1 in the lecture.
  • The lecture identifies mutations in the RYR1 gene.
  • Drug of choice: dantrolene.
If you see this, think this
Succinylcholine or inhalational anesthetic + hypermetabolic crisis → think malignant hyperthermia.
Hyperthermia is a late sign in the lecture.
Treatment anchor: dantrolene.

Botulinum toxin

  • Prevents release of acetylcholine from cholinergic vesicles.
  • Given by local injection for treatment of generalized spastic disorders every several weeks or months.
  • Most clinical studies described in the lecture use injection in one or two limbs.
  • Benefits last for weeks to months.
  • Type A botulinum toxin is used.
  • Botulinum toxin interferes with vesicle fusion by proteolytically cleaving SNAP proteins.
  • The lecture also notes local facial injection for short-term treatment of wrinkles and use for generalized spastic disorders such as cerebral palsy.
Acute local muscle spasm

Antispasmodics

p. 9

General characteristics

  • Used for acute local muscle spasm due to tissue trauma or muscle strain, such as whiplash injury.
  • The lecture states that these drugs are not listed in the Philippine National Formulary, 2017.
  • They are described as central-acting at the brainstem.
  • Examples: cyclobenzaprine, carisoprodol, chlorphenesin, chlorzoxazone, metaxalone, orphenadrine, methocarbamol.
  • Orphenadrine is noted as available in the Philippine market.

Cyclobenzaprine: prototype

  • Structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants.
  • Has antimuscarinic side effects.
  • Can cause sedation, transient visual hallucinations, and confusion.
  • Not given for UMN conditions such as spinal cord injury or cerebral palsy.
  • Abuse potential is present.
  • With serotonin-active drugs, the patient can develop serotonin syndrome.
  • Serotonin syndrome in the lecture can manifest as agitation, sweating, tremors, seizures, hyperthermia, and coma in severe cases.
  • Interacting drugs listed: SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, tramadol, bupropion, meperidine, verapamil, and MAO inhibitors.

Orphenadrine

  • Orally taken muscle relaxant.
  • In the Philippines, the lecture notes a combination with paracetamol called Norgesic.
  • In other regions, it may be combined with aspirin.
  • CNS effects: drowsiness, dizziness, blurred vision.
  • GI effects: dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, constipation.
  • CVS effects: tachycardia and palpitations.
Clinical pearl
17-year-old with spastic cerebral palsy: choose a spasmolytic, not a neuromuscular blocker. The lecture gives the route as oral.
30-year-old with severe upper-extremity muscle spasms after a fight: choose an antispasmodic.

Final rapid review

Cram Sheet

pp. 1–10

Neuromuscular transmission

  • Muscle receptor: NM nicotinic ligand-gated ion channel.
  • Adult subunits: 2α, β, γ, δ.
  • Two ACh sites: α-β and δ-α.
  • Two ACh molecules → channel opening → Na entry → depolarization → contraction.
  • AChE degrades ACh to choline + acetate.

Succinylcholine

  • Only clinically available depolarizing NMB in the lecture.
  • Onset 60–90 sec. Duration 5–10 min.
  • Plasma pseudocholinesterase → succinylmonocholine → succinic acid + choline.
  • Phase I: depolarization → fasciculations → flaccid paralysis.
  • Phase II: prolonged exposure → repolarized but desensitized membrane.
  • Neostigmine can prolong succinylcholine block.

Succinylcholine warnings

  • Hyperkalemia risk is emphasized with burns, trauma, nerve damage, neuromuscular disease, renal failure, metabolic acidosis.
  • ↑ intraocular pressure and ↑ intragastric pressure.
  • Fasciculations can cause postoperative myalgia.
  • Trigger for malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients.
  • Small nondepolarizing dose before succinylcholine can reduce fasciculations.

Pseudocholinesterase

  • Typical dibucaine number: 70–80.
  • Heterozygous atypical: 50–60, block ↑ about 50–100%.
  • Homozygous atypical: 20–30, block may last 4–8 h.
  • Pregnancy, burns, liver disease, neoplasia, and cholinesterase-inhibiting drugs can prolong block.

📌 Intermediate NdNMBs Nondepolarizing durations

  • Short: mivacurium 10–20 min.
  • Intermediate: atracurium, cisatracurium, rocuronium, vecuronium 20–35 min.
  • Long: pancuronium, tubocurarine >35 min.
  • Most clinically used NMBs in the lecture are intermediate duration.

📌 Hofmann elimination Nondepolarizing metabolism

  • Steroidal: hepatic metabolism.
  • 3-hydroxymetabolite: 40–80% potency of parent.
  • Atracurium and cisatracurium: hepatic + Hofmann elimination in plasma.
  • Laudanosine t½ about 150 min, crosses BBB, can accumulate with prolonged atracurium infusion.
  • Cisatracurium: less laudanosine and less histamine release.

Nondepolarizing mechanism and CVS

  • Main MOA: competitive antagonism at nAChR.
  • One blocker on one binding site can prevent channel opening.
  • 📌 Histamine Lecture states steroidal NMBs do not release histamine.
  • Histamine ranking: D-tubocurarine > metocurine > atracurium/mivacurium > cisatracurium.
  • Pancuronium: ↑ HR/CO ± ↑ SVR from vagolytic action, NE release, and blocked NE uptake.

📌 Special populations Special populations

  • Myasthenia gravis: less susceptible to depolarizing NMBs, more susceptible to nondepolarizing NMBs.
  • Severe burns or UMN disease: avoid depolarizing NMBs. Relative resistance to nondepolarizers from extrajunctional receptor proliferation.
  • Elderly >70: decreased liver and kidney clearance → prolonged action → lower nondepolarizing doses.

📌 TOF thresholds Monitoring

  • No drug: 4 equal twitches.
  • Nondepolarizing block: fade.
  • Depolarizing block: equal diminution.
  • TOFR 0 → complete paralysis and best time for intubation in the lecture.
  • TOFR >90% → recovery from neuromuscular blockade.

Sugammadex

  • Steroidal NdNMB reversal: rocuronium, vecuronium, pancuronium.
  • 1:1 tight binding in plasma.
  • 18× faster onset than neostigmine in the lecture.
  • Excreted in urine within 24 h with normal renal function.
  • 📌 Renal impairment Severe renal impairment → complex remains longer in plasma.
  • 📌 Adverse effects Hypersensitivity, anaphylaxis, rare bradycardia/cardiac arrest, coagulopathy.
  • Progesterone contraceptives: effect like missing 1–2 doses. Use alternative non-progesterone contraception for 7 days.

📌 Spasmolytics vs antispasmodics Spasmolytics

  • Spasmolytics → UMN-related spasticity.
  • 📌 Central Central: diazepam, baclofen, tizanidine.
  • 📌 Peripheral Peripheral: dantrolene, eperisone, pherinamidol.
  • Diazepam → GABAA.
  • Baclofen → GABAB, less sedation than diazepam.
  • Tizanidine → α2, hypotension.
  • Dantrolene → SR Ca release inhibition via RYR1.

📌 Other central spasmolytics Other lecture-listed agents

  • Gabapentin and pregabalin: voltage-gated Ca++ channel antagonism.
  • Progabide: GABAA and GABAB agonist.
  • Glycine: inhibitory amino acid neurotransmitter with more spinal action.
  • Idrocilamide and riluzole: inhibit glutamatergic transmission and are discussed for ALS.

Malignant hyperthermia

  • Triggers: succinylcholine and inhalational anesthetics.
  • Uncontrolled SR Ca release → hypermetabolic state.
  • ↑ CO2, ↑ pCO2, acidosis, arrhythmias.
  • Hyperthermia is a late sign.
  • Chromosome 19q13.1, RYR1 mutation.
  • Dantrolene = drug of choice.

Antispasmodics

  • Used for acute local muscle spasm from peripheral musculoskeletal conditions.
  • Cyclobenzaprine = prototype.
  • Cyclobenzaprine is related to TCAs and has antimuscarinic effects.
  • With serotonin-active drugs → serotonin syndrome.
  • Orphenadrine in the Philippines is noted in a paracetamol combination called Norgesic.
